text: I want you to meet Helen.
Helen is my partner in life and work
and usually my copresenter.
So she sends her regrets that she's not here today,
but you'll learn more about her as I tell you our story.
And I want to start our story
with the fact that we have been married now for 44 years.
And -- thank you.
(Applause)
But during that time, we considered divorce several times.

in our relationship

we had to listen to that diagnosis,

The methodology was that we were going to monitor ourselves daily

Now the conversation that we agreed to was not just an ordinary conversation.
The ordinary conversation is just what we all do.
They're called parallel monologues.
And that in which
you talk and the other person talks
and you're trying to control the narrative,
or you're waiting for the other person to stop
so you can refute their commitment to their absolute truth.
(Laughter)
(Laughter)
Our conversation was going to be a dialogical conversation.
By the way, the monological conversation is vertical and top-down.
So the dialogical conversation is lateral.
Everybody is equal.
So that we call a dialogical conversation,
and we define dialogical conversation
as two people listening without criticizing,
talking without criticizing, listening without judgment,
talking without criticizing, listening without judgment,
and connecting beyond your differences.
So it's a powerful conversation.
It has a structure
and you have to go through this structure.
It starts with an appointment.
You always ask, "Is now a good time to talk?"
Then you go through three steps in the structure,
which is mirroring.
Mirroring is what turns listening into engagement.
Then you go through a validation process
Then you go through a validation process
in which you differentiate from each other.
So each can have an affirmation of the correctness
of their separate points of view
that it is possible to do that.
And then you do empathy in which you express your acceptance of
and experience of their feelings and then a connecting process.
So we had three topics to run through that
and we had now a year to do that.
So the first topic was,
So the first topic was,
“How are we feeling in our relationship?”
So I asked Helen that, and she asked me that.
And after a few weeks of talking,
it got really clear that neither of us felt safe
or visible in our relationship.
So that was striking that we both felt the same way
and with the same intensity.
So we wondered, is this connected to our childhoods?
Because as a therapist,
childhood is the source of everything
childhood is the source of everything
that shows up in adulthood as something that you don't really want.
(Laughter)
So we found that it really was.
I grew up on a farm,
to parents who were sharecroppers,
and both of them died before I was six,
and I was reared by my older sisters, of whom I had three,
and they passed me around because they were poor
and could keep me only for a little while.
and could keep me only for a little while.
So I didn't feel visible in my growing up.
And Helen,
on the other end of the economic and social spectrum,
grew up in a mansion.
Her parents were busy making money,
wealth and doing philanthropy.
And so there were maids who ran her house,
and their job was to also care for her.
And so she felt essentially invisible to her parents.
So that invisibility was there.

We really don’t know each other really very well.
We know and have been relating to each other's professional personas,
to our defenses and how we protect ourselves,
but we haven't really felt safe enough to be who we really are.
And in the process of talking and listening,

and that we sort of liked each other.

We had X's all over the calendar.
So we decided to add a new quality called appreciation,
so that we would give each other appreciations on a daily basis.
And also we were sort of serious, so we injected humor.
Next three months we took an evaluation of our relationship

So this was getting to be challenging and puzzling for us.

Why were we holding on to negativity?
So we made a radical decision
that our marriage, as a system, required negativity,
and that what we needed to do was change the system itself
into another system which would not require negativity.
Because the system we were in,
we saw each other as resources for each other
we saw each other as resources for each other
and therefore, as a resource,
you're always going to not fulfill the deal,
and there will always be a basis then for frustration and criticism.
But we decided we would change the perception of each other
from a resource
into a blessing or a gift.
And that we would base that on the fact that each of us were
creatures of nature,
creatures of nature,
that each of us had intrinsic value
and that we were valuable because we existed
and that we would honor that value, because we existed.
And so practicing that for the next three months,
our impasse resolved,
we began to feel safe with each other and seen by each other.
Our problems became decisions to make
rather than issues to debate.
So we were at the end of that process, and that was 26 years ago.

so we went back into the public life.
So what we want to say in conclusion
is that over
about 10 or 12 years ago,
we moved dialogue from couples into the world

[and] found it works equally well there.
So we launched, 12 years ago, a global social movement
So we launched, 12 years ago, a global social movement
to teach dialogue
to 2.4 billion people in the world by 2050 --
which is the tipping point of the world’s population on that day
in order to usher in a relational civilization
in which everybody will relate laterally and equally,
and everybody will be seen,
heard, valued and included.
So we wind up with these three affirmations.
So we wind up with these three affirmations.
One is, you cannot love whom you do not know --
and you cannot know without listening.
So that listening is the first act of love.
This is available to anyone.
And as we have experienced,
it's never too late to start listening and loving.
